dp[i][j] = minimum operations to turn the first i chars of A into the first j chars of B. Transition: if chars match, dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).
How does the O(n log n) LIS work?
Maintain an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each element, binary-search its position in tails and overwrite (or append). The length of tails at the end is the LIS length.
When do you need bitmask DP?
When a subproblem is identified by "which subset of a small set (≤ ~20 elements) has been used/visited" — TSP, assignment problems, "partition into groups". The state count is 2ⁿ.
Memoisation vs tabulation trade-off?
Memoisation computes only reachable states and is easy to write from the recurrence, but has recursion overhead and stack-depth limits. Tabulation visits all states in a fixed order, enabling tight loops and O(1)-row space, at the cost of sometimes computing states you don't need.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does dp[i][j] usually represent in a two-string DP?
The answer for the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other.
Time complexity of the classic 0/1 knapsack DP?
O(n × W) where n = items, W = capacity. (Pseudo-polynomial — exponential in the number of bits of W.)
Coin change "number of ways": iterate coins outer or inner?
Coins outer, amount inner — this counts combinations (order doesn't matter). Swapping the loops counts permutations.

Intermediate core

Longest common subsequence recurrence.
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if A[i-1] == B[j-1], else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base: dp[0][*] = dp[*][0] = 0. O(nm) time; O(min(n,m)) space with rolling rows (but you lose easy reconstruction).
House robber on a binary tree (can't rob adjacent nodes). State & transition?
Post-order; each node returns a pair (rob, skip). skip = max(childL) + max(childR) (children free to do anything). rob = node.val + skip_of(L) + skip_of(R). Answer = max of the root's pair. O(n).

Advanced deep

Explain "burst balloons" (interval DP) — why the natural "which balloon to burst first" framing fails and the fix.
If you define dp by the first balloon burst in a range, the subranges become non-contiguous and coupled (bursting one changes the neighbours of others). The fix: define dp[i][j] for the open interval (i, j) and iterate over which balloon k is burst last in that interval. When k is last, its neighbours are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j, and the left and right sub-intervals (i, k) and (k, j) are independent. Transition: dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j]. O(n³). The "think about the last operation, not the first" reframing is a recurring interval-DP trick (also matrix-chain, optimal BST).
How does digit DP count integers in [0, N] with some digit property?
Process the number left to right, digit position by position. State: (pos, tight, ...propertyState), where tight means the prefix built so far equals N's prefix (so the current digit is capped at N's digit; otherwise it can be 0–9). Memoise on (pos, tight=false, propertyState) — the tight=true path is a single chain and not cached. Add a started/leadingZero flag if leading zeros need special handling. At pos == len, return 1 if the property holds. Complexity O(len × 10 × #propertyStates). Handles "count numbers with digit sum S", "no two equal adjacent digits", "≤ K distinct digits", etc.

Graph Traversal Applications

What you can actually do once you can BFS and DFS a graph.

Notes

Flood fill / grid as graph

Treat a grid cell as a node with up-to-4 (or 8) neighbours. BFS/DFS from a cell to fill a region, count islands, find the shortest path in a maze (BFS), or expand from multiple sources at once (multi-source BFS: seed the queue with all sources — "rotting oranges", "walls and gates", "01 matrix").

Connectivity

  • Connected components (undirected): loop vertices, BFS/DFS each unvisited one, count.
  • Strongly connected components (directed): Tarjan (one DFS, low-link) or Kosaraju (DFS, transpose, DFS by finish order).
  • Bipartite check: 2-colour via BFS/DFS; a same-colour edge → not bipartite.

Cycle detection

  • Undirected: DFS — a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means a cycle. Or union-find.
  • Directed: 3-colour DFS (edge to a grey node = back edge = cycle), or Kahn's topological sort leaving nodes unplaced.

DFS tree structure

DFS classifies edges (tree / back / forward / cross) and computes disc[] (discovery time) and low[] (earliest reachable ancestor). From these:

  • Bridges — edge (u, v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u].
  • Articulation points — removing them disconnects the graph; found via the same low-link condition (with a root special case).
Cheat Sheet
  • Grid problems: cell = node, 4/8 neighbours. BFS for shortest steps, DFS/BFS for region fill.
  • Multi-source BFS: push all sources first, then standard BFS → nearest-source distance for every cell.
  • Connected components: iterate + BFS/DFS unvisited; SCC via Tarjan (1 pass) or Kosaraju (2 passes + transpose).
  • Bipartite: 2-colouring; conflict edge → no.
  • Undirected cycle: DFS visited-non-parent, or union-find. Directed cycle: grey back-edge, or Kahn leftovers.
  • Bridges / articulation points: DFS with disc[] and low[]; low[v] > disc[u] → bridge.
  • Topological order (DAG): Kahn (in-degree queue) or DFS finish-time reverse.
  • All these are O(V + E) on an adjacency list.
Q&A
How do you count islands in a grid of land/water?
Scan cells; on each unvisited land cell, run BFS/DFS to mark its whole connected region, and increment a counter. O(rows × cols).
What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
BFS started from many sources simultaneously (all pushed into the queue before the loop). Every node's first visit gives its distance to the nearest source. Used for "how far is each cell from the closest exit/fire/gate".
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
DFS with three states: unvisited, in-progress (on the current recursion path), done. An edge to an in-progress node is a back edge, so there's a cycle. Alternatively, if Kahn's topological sort can't place all V nodes, a cycle exists.
What is low[v] in bridge-finding?
The smallest discovery time reachable from v's DFS subtree using tree edges plus at most one back edge. If a child v of u has low[v] > disc[u], no back edge from v's subtree bypasses the edge (u, v), so it's a bridge.
Kosaraju vs Tarjan for SCCs?
Both are O(V + E). Kosaraju: DFS to get finish order, build the transpose graph, DFS in reverse finish order — two passes, conceptually simple. Tarjan: a single DFS maintaining a stack and low-links — one pass, less memory (no transpose), slightly trickier to implement.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which traversal gives shortest path in an unweighted maze?
BFS.
How do you check if a graph is bipartite?
Try to 2-colour it with BFS/DFS; if any edge connects two same-coloured nodes, it isn't bipartite.
Complexity of BFS/DFS on an adjacency list?
O(V + E).

Intermediate core

Course schedule: given prerequisites, can all courses be finished?
Build a directed graph course → dependent. Run Kahn's topological sort (or 3-colour DFS). If you can order all courses (no cycle), yes; a cycle means an impossible circular dependency. O(V + E).
Rotting oranges: minutes until no fresh orange remains (or -1).
Multi-source BFS from all initially-rotten oranges. Each BFS "level" is one minute; rot fresh neighbours and enqueue them. The answer is the number of levels processed; if any fresh orange is still unreached, return -1. O(rows × cols).

Advanced deep

Find all bridges in an undirected graph in one DFS. Give the core condition and an edge case.
DFS assigning disc[u] (entry time) and low[u] = min(disc[u], disc of nodes reachable via one back edge from u's subtree). For a tree edge (u, v): after returning from v, set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); if low[v] > disc[u], edge (u, v) is a bridge. Edge case: when relaxing, skip the immediate parent edge once (not all edges to the parent) — with parallel edges between u and its parent, the second such edge is a valid back edge and prevents both from being bridges. Track parent by edge id, not just node id. O(V + E).
Explain the 2-SAT → SCC reduction.
A 2-SAT formula (clauses of ≤ 2 literals) is satisfiable iff no variable x has both x and ¬x in the same strongly connected component of the "implication graph". Build the graph: each clause (a ∨ b) becomes two edges ¬a → b and ¬b → a (if a is false then b must be true, and vice versa). Run an SCC algorithm (Tarjan). If x and ¬x share a component → UNSAT. Otherwise assign each variable by comparing the SCC (in reverse topological / component order) of x vs ¬x — the literal whose component comes later is true. O(n + m). This turns a satisfiability problem into linear-time graph work.

Shortest Paths

Pick the algorithm by edge weights: unweighted, non-negative, negative, or all-pairs.

Notes

The decision table

SituationAlgorithmTime
Unweighted (or all equal weights)BFSO(V + E)
Weights 0/10-1 BFS (deque)O(V + E)
Non-negative weights, single sourceDijkstra (binary heap)O((V + E) log V)
Negative weights allowed, single sourceBellman-FordO(V · E)
All pairs, dense, small VFloyd-WarshallO(V³)
Goal-directed with a heuristicA*≤ Dijkstra in practice

Dijkstra

Grow a set of finalised nodes; repeatedly take the unfinalised node with the smallest tentative distance (min-heap), finalise it, and relax its outgoing edges. Correct only for non-negative weights — a negative edge could improve an already-finalised node. Use lazy deletion (push duplicates, skip stale pops) rather than decrease-key.

Bellman-Ford

Relax all edges V - 1 times (the longest simple path has ≤ V-1 edges). A further relaxation that still improves something → a negative cycle reachable from the source. Slower but handles negatives and detects negative cycles.

Floyd-Warshall

for k in V:
  for i in V:
    for j in V:
      dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])

k is "intermediate vertices allowed so far". Handles negative edges (no negative cycles); dist[i][i] < 0 afterward flags a negative cycle through i.

A*

Dijkstra with priority g(n) + h(n), where h estimates the remaining distance to the goal. If h is admissible (never overestimates) the result is optimal; if also consistent, no node is expanded twice. A good heuristic (e.g. straight-line distance on a map) massively prunes the search.

Cheat Sheet
  • Unweighted → BFS. 0/1 weights → 0-1 BFS (deque, push_front for 0).
  • Non-negative weights → Dijkstra + min-heap, O((V+E) log V). Lazy deletion over decrease-key.
  • Negative edges → Bellman-Ford, O(VE); extra relaxation succeeds → negative cycle.
  • All pairs → Floyd-Warshall O(V³) (or Dijkstra from each source for sparse graphs; Johnson's for sparse + negatives).
  • Dijkstra is wrong with any negative edge.
  • A* = Dijkstra with f = g + h; admissible h → optimal; consistent h → no re-expansion.
  • Reconstruct paths via a prev[] / parent array updated on each successful relaxation.
Q&A
Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edge weights?
It finalises the closest node and never revisits it. A negative edge encountered later could create a shorter path to that already-finalised node, which Dijkstra can't account for.
How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?
After V-1 rounds of relaxing all edges, shortest paths are final if no negative cycle exists. If a V-th round still relaxes some edge, a reachable negative cycle must exist.
What does the outer loop variable k mean in Floyd-Warshall?
"Consider paths whose intermediate vertices are all in {0, …, k}." After the loop finishes for all k, every vertex is allowed as an intermediate, so dist holds true shortest paths.
When is A* just Dijkstra?
When the heuristic h is 0 everywhere — then priority is just g(n), the known distance, which is Dijkstra.
Single-source shortest path on a DAG — anything faster than Dijkstra?
Yes: topologically sort, then relax edges in that order — O(V + E), and it handles negative weights (no cycles possible).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Best algorithm for shortest path with all edge weights = 1?
BFS — O(V + E), simpler and faster than Dijkstra.
Dijkstra's time complexity with a binary heap?
O((V + E) log V).
Which algorithm gives all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³)?
Floyd-Warshall.

Intermediate core

Implement Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion.
Push (0, source). While the heap is non-empty, pop (d, u); if d > dist[u] skip (stale). Otherwise for each edge (u, v, w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v). No need to remove old entries — the staleness check handles them. Heap can hold up to O(E) entries.
Cheapest flights within K stops (weighted graph, stop limit). Approach?
Bellman-Ford limited to K + 1 relaxation rounds — each round allows one more edge (stop). Crucially, relax from a snapshot of distances at the start of each round so a single round can't chain multiple edges. Or a BFS/Dijkstra-style search with state (node, stopsUsed).

Advanced deep

What is Johnson's algorithm and when does it beat Floyd-Warshall?
All-pairs shortest paths for graphs with negative edges but no negative cycles, on sparse graphs. Step 1: add a virtual node with 0-weight edges to all vertices; run Bellman-Ford from it to get h(v) for every vertex. Step 2: reweight each edge w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v), which is provably non-negative and preserves shortest paths. Step 3: run Dijkstra from every source on the reweighted graph, then subtract the offset. Total O(VE + V·E log V) = O(VE log V), which beats Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) when E « V².
Prove Dijkstra's correctness for non-negative weights (sketch).
Invariant: when a node u is popped/finalised, dist[u] is its true shortest distance. Suppose not — let u be the first finalised node with dist[u] > δ(s, u). Consider a true shortest path s → … → u; let y be the first node on it not yet finalised, with finalised predecessor x. Since x was finalised correctly, dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + w(x,y) = δ(s, y) (relaxed when x was processed). Because edge weights are non-negative, δ(s, y) ≤ δ(s, u) < dist[u]. So dist[y] < dist[u], meaning the heap would have popped y before u — contradiction. Non-negativity is essential in the δ(s,y) ≤ δ(s,u) step.

MST & Topological Sort

Cheapest connecting tree, and ordering a dependency graph.

Notes

Minimum Spanning Tree

A subset of edges connecting all V vertices with no cycle and minimum total weight (exactly V - 1 edges). Both standard algorithms are greedy, justified by the cut property: for any partition of the vertices, the lightest edge crossing it is in some MST.

KruskalPrim
Ideasort all edges; add the next lightest that doesn't form a cyclegrow a tree from a start vertex, always adding the lightest edge leaving it
Cycle checkunion-finda "visited" set
TimeO(E log E)O((V + E) log V) with a heap; O(V²) with an array (good for dense)
Best forsparse graphs, edge list givendense graphs

Topological sort

A linear order of a DAG's vertices such that every edge u → v has u before v. Not unique. Two methods:

  • Kahn's (BFS): repeatedly remove a vertex with in-degree 0, decrementing its successors. If fewer than V vertices come out → there's a cycle.
  • DFS: push each vertex onto a stack when its DFS finishes; the reversed stack is a topological order.

Uses: build systems (make), task/course scheduling, spreadsheet recalculation, package managers, resolving symbol dependencies at link time.

Related

Longest path in a DAG = topological order + DP relax (the general longest-path problem is NP-hard, but a DAG makes it linear). Lexicographically smallest topological order = Kahn's with a min-heap instead of a queue.

Cheat Sheet
  • MST: V-1 edges, connected, acyclic, minimum total weight. Greedy works via the cut property.
  • Kruskal: sort edges, add if endpoints in different DSU sets, union. O(E log E). Sparse / edge list.
  • Prim: heap of frontier edges, grow one tree. O((V+E) log V) heap or O(V²) array. Dense.
  • Both give the same total weight; the tree itself may differ if weights tie.
  • Topological sort needs a DAG; result not unique.
  • Kahn's: in-degree-0 queue; leftover vertices → cycle. DFS: reverse of finish order.
  • Lexicographically smallest topo order → Kahn's with a min-heap.
  • DAG longest/shortest path: process in topological order, relax — O(V + E).
Q&A
State the cut property.
For any cut (partition of vertices into two non-empty sets), the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST. This is what makes greedily adding safe edges correct.
Kruskal vs Prim — when to use each?
Kruskal when the graph is sparse or given as an edge list (sort edges, union-find). Prim when the graph is dense (its O(V²) array version beats sorting O(V²) edges) or given as an adjacency structure.
What data structure makes Kruskal efficient?
Union-Find (disjoint set) — O(α(V)) per "are these connected / union them" check while scanning sorted edges.
Can topological sort be applied to any directed graph?
No — only a DAG. If the graph has a directed cycle, no valid linear order exists (and both Kahn's and DFS can detect that).
Is a topological ordering unique?
Generally no. It's unique iff at every step there's exactly one vertex with in-degree 0 (equivalently, the DAG has a Hamiltonian path).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many edges in an MST of a connected graph with V vertices?
Exactly V − 1.
Which algorithm pairs with union-find?
Kruskal's MST.
What does Kahn's algorithm start with?
All vertices that have in-degree 0.

Intermediate core

Implement Kruskal's algorithm.
Sort edges by weight ascending. Initialise a DSU over V vertices. For each edge (u, v, w) in order: if find(u) != find(v), add the edge to the MST and union(u, v). Stop when you've added V − 1 edges. O(E log E) dominated by the sort.
Return the lexicographically smallest valid course order.
Kahn's algorithm but with a min-heap of the currently-available (in-degree 0) vertices instead of a plain queue. Always take the smallest-numbered available vertex next. O((V + E) log V).

Advanced deep

How do you find a minimum spanning tree that must include a given edge, or exclude one?
Must include edge e: contract e (union its endpoints first / add it to the tree with weight treated as −∞), then run Kruskal/Prim on the rest. Must exclude e: run the MST algorithm skipping e. For "is edge e in every MST / some MST": e is in some MST iff it's a minimum-weight edge across some cut (equivalently, in the graph of edges with weight < w(e), its endpoints are in different components); e is in every MST iff it's the unique lightest edge across some cut (no alternative equal-weight edge closes the same cycle). These are the basis of MST sensitivity analysis.
Prove Prim's algorithm produces a minimum spanning tree.
Loop invariant: the set of edges chosen so far, A, is a subset of some MST. Initially A = ∅ — true. Inductive step: Prim adds the lightest edge (u, v) crossing the cut (S, V\S) where S is the current tree's vertices. By the cut property, this lightest crossing edge is in some MST T. If (u, v) ∈ T, A ∪ {(u,v)} is still a subset of T. If not, T ∪ {(u,v)} has a cycle containing another edge (x, y) crossing the cut; w(x,y) ≥ w(u,v), so swapping gives an MST T' containing A ∪ {(u,v)} with weight ≤ w(T). Either way the invariant holds. After V-1 edges, A is a spanning tree that is a subset of an MST — hence is an MST.

String Matching

Finding a pattern in text faster than the O(nm) nested loop.

Notes

Naive

For each of the n - m + 1 alignments, compare up to m characters. O(nm) worst case (e.g. text aaaa…a, pattern aaa…ab). Fine for short patterns / small text.

Rabin-Karp (rolling hash)

  • Hash the pattern and each length-m window of the text; compare hashes, verify on match.
  • The rolling hash updates in O(1) as the window slides: h = (h - text[i]·b^(m-1))·b + text[i+m], all mod a large prime.
  • O(n + m) average; O(nm) worst case if many hash collisions (mitigate with a good modulus / double hashing).
  • Shines for multiple pattern search (hash all patterns, one text pass) and 2-D pattern matching.

KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt)

  • Precompute the prefix function π[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix.
  • On a mismatch after matching k chars, don't restart — jump the pattern to π[k-1], reusing the known match.
  • The text pointer never moves backward → O(n + m) guaranteed, O(m) extra space.
# prefix function
π = [0]*m; k = 0
for i in 1..m-1:
    while k > 0 and p[i] != p[k]: k = π[k-1]
    if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
    π[i] = k

Z-algorithm

Computes Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. Run on pattern + separator + text; any Z[i] ≥ m in the text part is a match. O(n + m), often simpler to reason about than KMP.

Cheat Sheet
  • Naive: O(nm) worst, O(1) space, fine for small inputs.
  • Rabin-Karp: rolling hash, O(n + m) average, great for many patterns / 2-D; verify on hash hit.
  • KMP: prefix function π, O(n + m) worst case, text pointer never backtracks.
  • Z-algorithm: Z[i] = prefix-match length at i; run on P + '#' + T; O(n + m).
  • Aho-Corasick: KMP generalised to a trie of many patterns — all matches in O(n + total pattern length + #matches).
  • Boyer-Moore (bad-char + good-suffix): sublinear average, used by grep; skips ahead from the end of the pattern.
  • Suffix automaton / suffix array: preprocess the text once, then answer many pattern queries fast.
Q&A
What does the KMP prefix function store?
π[i] = the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch it tells you how far you can shift the pattern without missing a match.
Why is KMP O(n + m) and not O(nm)?
The text index only ever moves forward. Each character is compared a bounded number of times because failed matches fall back via π rather than re-scanning the text.
What is a rolling hash?
A hash of a sliding window that can be updated in O(1) when the window shifts by one — subtract the outgoing character's contribution, multiply by the base, add the incoming character (all modulo a large prime).
Rabin-Karp's worst case and when it hits.
O(nm) — when the hash collides at (almost) every window so you keep doing full O(m) verifications. Rare with a good random modulus; adversarial input can force it, mitigated by double hashing or a secret modulus.
When would you choose Rabin-Karp over KMP?
Searching for many patterns at once (hash them all, one text pass), 2-D pattern matching, or when you need "any of these substrings" checks — the hash comparison generalises where KMP's single-pattern automaton doesn't.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Worst-case time of naive substring search?
O(nm) — text length n, pattern length m.
KMP's overall complexity?
O(n + m), guaranteed.
Which algorithm uses a rolling hash?
Rabin-Karp.

Intermediate core

Compute the prefix function for "ababaca".
Index: a b a b a c a → π = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1]. At index 4 ("ababa"), the longest prefix=suffix is "aba" (length 3); the "c" breaks it back to 0; the final "a" matches the prefix "a" (length 1).
Find the shortest palindrome by adding characters only to the front.
Build s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute its prefix function; the last value k is the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s. Prepend the reverse of s[k:]. O(n). (Same result via the Z-algorithm or Manacher.)

Advanced deep

Describe Aho-Corasick and its complexity for matching many patterns.
Build a trie of all patterns. Add failure links: from each node, a pointer to the longest proper suffix of the string-so-far that is also a trie node (computed by a BFS over the trie, exactly the multi-pattern generalisation of KMP's π). Also add output links so that when you land on a node you can enumerate every pattern that ends there or at a suffix. Then scan the text once, following child edges or failure links on mismatch, emitting matches. Total: O(Σ pattern lengths) to build + O(text length + number of matches) to search. It's what tools like fgrep -f patterns.txt, intrusion-detection signature scanners, and spam filters use.
How does a suffix array answer "does P occur in T" and how is it built efficiently?
A suffix array is the sorted order of all n suffixes of T (stored as their start indices). Since the suffixes are sorted, every occurrence of a pattern P corresponds to suffixes with P as a prefix — a contiguous block — found by two binary searches for the lower/upper bound of P, each doing O(m) character comparisons: O(m log n) per query (O(m + log n) with an LCP array). Construction: the naive "sort the suffixes" is O(n² log n); the prefix-doubling method sorts by first 2^k characters in rounds using radix sort, O(n log n) (or O(n log² n) simpler); SA-IS achieves O(n). Suffix arrays use far less memory than suffix trees and are the practical choice for large-text indexing (bioinformatics, full-text search, BWT/bzip2).

Relational Model, Keys & Constraints

Tables as sets of tuples, and the keys that give rows identity and link them together.

Notes

The model

A relation (table) is a set of tuples (rows) over named, typed attributes (columns). Rows are unordered and, in the pure model, unique. SQL relaxes this (bag semantics — duplicates allowed unless a key forbids them).

Keys

KeyMeaning
Super keyAny attribute set that uniquely identifies a row.
Candidate keyA minimal super key (no attribute can be removed).
Primary keyThe chosen candidate key; implies NOT NULL + UNIQUE, usually the clustering key.
Alternate keyA candidate key not chosen as primary.
Foreign keyAttribute(s) referencing another table's primary/unique key — enforces referential integrity.
Composite keyA key spanning multiple columns.

Natural key = meaningful data (email, ISBN). Surrogate key = a synthetic id (auto-increment, UUID) — stable, uniform, no business meaning. Most schemas use surrogates as primary keys and enforce natural keys with UNIQUE constraints.

Constraints

  • NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY (with ON DELETE/UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION).
  • CHECK (domain rules, e.g. price >= 0), DEFAULT.
  • Constraints move integrity rules into the DB so every writer obeys them, not just the app.

NULL

Means "unknown / not applicable", not zero or empty string. Three-valued logic: NULL = NULL is unknown (not true); use IS NULL. Aggregates skip NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULLs.

Cheat Sheet
  • Relation = set of tuples over typed attributes; rows unordered.
  • Super key ⊇ candidate key (minimal) → one chosen as primary key (NOT NULL + UNIQUE).
  • Foreign key → references another table's key; enforces referential integrity; choose ON DELETE behaviour deliberately.
  • Surrogate key (auto id / UUID) as PK + UNIQUE on the natural key is the common pattern.
  • Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, PRIMARY/FOREIGN KEY.
  • NULL = unknown; comparisons yield unknown; use IS [NOT] NULL; 3-valued logic.
  • COUNT(*) = rows; COUNT(col) = non-NULL values.
Q&A
Candidate key vs primary key?
A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies rows; a table can have several. The primary key is the one you designate as the row's official identifier — it becomes NOT NULL and typically the clustering key.
Surrogate vs natural key — trade-offs?
Natural keys carry meaning and avoid an extra column, but can change (someone's email), may be wide/composite (slower joins, bigger indexes), and can leak data. Surrogates are stable, compact, uniform, and meaningless — at the cost of an extra column and a join to get human-readable identity.
What does a foreign key enforce?
Referential integrity: a child row's FK value must match an existing parent key (or be NULL). The ON DELETE/ON UPDATE action defines what happens to children when the parent changes.
Why is WHERE col = NULL wrong?
Comparing anything to NULL yields unknown, which the WHERE clause treats as not-true, so the row is excluded. Use WHERE col IS NULL.
Where should data-integrity rules live — app or database?
Core invariants belong in the database as constraints, so they hold regardless of which application, script, or admin writes the data. The app can add friendlier validation on top, but shouldn't be the only guard.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What two properties does a primary key imply?
NOT NULL and UNIQUE.
What does a foreign key point to?
A primary key (or unique key) in another (or the same) table.
Difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(email)?
COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(email) counts rows where email is not NULL.

Intermediate core

You delete a customer who has orders. What are the FK options and their effects?
RESTRICT/NO ACTION: the delete fails while orders reference them. CASCADE: the orders are deleted too. SET NULL: the orders' customer_id becomes NULL (orphaned but kept). SET DEFAULT: set to a default customer. Choice depends on whether order history must survive customer deletion.
Why can composite natural keys hurt performance as a primary key?
Every secondary index and every child table's FK stores a copy of the full PK. A wide composite key (several columns, strings) bloats those indexes and FK columns, makes joins compare more bytes, and worsens cache/page utilisation. A narrow surrogate (4–8 byte integer) keeps indexes and joins tight.

Advanced deep

Discuss auto-increment integer vs UUID vs ULID as a surrogate primary key at scale.
Auto-increment int/bigint: smallest, fastest joins, and monotonic so inserts append to the end of a clustered index (no page splits) — but reveals row counts, needs coordination across shards/nodes (a central sequence or ranges), and complicates multi-master. Random UUID v4: globally unique with no coordination, safe to expose — but 16 bytes, and randomness scatters inserts across the clustered index causing page splits, fragmentation, and worse cache locality; also poor as a covering-index prefix. ULID / UUID v7 (time-ordered): keeps global uniqueness and non-coordination while restoring insert locality by prefixing a timestamp, so it's become the preferred distributed-friendly choice. Rule: single-node OLTP → bigint; distributed / offline-generated ids → time-ordered UUID.
What is referential integrity's interaction with concurrent transactions and deferred constraints?
By default FK checks are immediate (checked at each statement), which can force an awkward insert order for cyclic references (A references B and B references A). DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraints are checked only at COMMIT, letting you insert both rows then commit. Concurrency: a transaction inserting a child takes a shared/key-share lock on the referenced parent row so another transaction can't delete it before commit — this can cause lock contention or deadlocks on hot parent rows (e.g. a "everything references the same tenant" row). Mitigations: deferred constraints, avoiding needless FKs on ultra-hot rows, or application-level integrity where the contention cost outweighs the safety.

Normalization (1NF to BCNF)

Removing redundancy so an update can't leave the data contradicting itself.

Notes

The anomalies normalization prevents

  • Update anomaly — a fact stored in many rows; updating one misses the others.
  • Insertion anomaly — can't record fact A without also knowing unrelated fact B.
  • Deletion anomaly — deleting a row loses an unrelated fact.

Functional dependencies

X → Y: X determines Y (same X always has the same Y). Normalization is about making every non-key attribute depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

The normal forms

FormRequires
1NFAtomic values, no repeating groups / arrays-in-a-column; each row unique.
2NF1NF + no non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key (no partial dependency).
3NF2NF + no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependency).
BCNFFor every FD X → Y, X is a super key. Stricter than 3NF; matters when there are overlapping candidate keys.

Higher: 4NF (multivalued dependencies), 5NF (join dependencies) — rarely cited in interviews.

Denormalization

Deliberately reintroducing redundancy (duplicated columns, precomputed aggregates, wide "read models") to cut join cost on read-heavy workloads — at the cost of write complexity and the anomalies you must now handle in application code or triggers. Common in reporting tables, caches, and NoSQL document design. Normalize first; denormalize with evidence.

Cheat Sheet
  • Goal: every non-key column depends on "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key".
  • 1NF: atomic cells, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on part of a composite key.
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency (non-key → non-key).
  • BCNF: every determinant is a super key (stricter; needed with overlapping candidate keys).
  • Normalization removes update/insert/delete anomalies and redundancy.
  • Denormalize only for measured read performance; then own the consistency cost.
  • OLTP → normalized; OLAP / analytics → star schema (denormalized dimensions).
Q&A
What problem does normalization solve?
Redundancy and the resulting update/insert/delete anomalies — storing a fact in one place so it can't become inconsistent.
What is a partial dependency (2NF violation)?
A non-key attribute that depends on only part of a composite primary key. E.g. key = (order_id, product_id), and product_name depends only on product_id — move it to a products table.
What is a transitive dependency (3NF violation)?
A non-key attribute determined by another non-key attribute. E.g. key = employee_id, and department_name depends on department_id (also non-key) — split departments out.
3NF vs BCNF?
3NF allows an FD X → Y where X isn't a super key if Y is part of some candidate key. BCNF forbids that entirely: every determinant must be a super key. They differ only when candidate keys overlap.
When is denormalization justified?
Read-heavy workloads where join/aggregate cost dominates and the write path can absorb the extra work of keeping duplicates in sync (via app logic, triggers, or materialized views). Analytics/reporting and document stores routinely denormalize.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does 1NF require?
Atomic column values — no lists, arrays, or repeating groups in a single field — and uniquely identifiable rows.
Name the three anomalies.
Update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.
Which normal form removes transitive dependencies?
3NF.

Intermediate core

A table (student_id, course_id, student_name, grade) with PK (student_id, course_id). Which NF is violated and how do you fix it?
2NF — student_name depends only on student_id, part of the composite key (partial dependency). Split into students(student_id, student_name) and enrollments(student_id, course_id, grade).
Give an example where a schema is in 3NF but not BCNF.
(student, subject, teacher) where each teacher teaches one subject, and each (student, subject) pair has one teacher. Candidate keys: (student, subject) and (student, teacher). FD teacher → subject holds, but teacher is not a super key → not BCNF. It is 3NF because subject is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF decomposition: (teacher, subject) and (student, teacher).

Advanced deep

BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation. Explain the trade-off with 3NF.
Every schema can be decomposed into BCNF losslessly (you can rejoin without spurious rows), but not always in a way that lets every original functional dependency be checked within a single resulting table — some FDs become "inter-table", enforceable only with a join or an assertion. 3NF decomposition (via the synthesis algorithm from a minimal cover) is always both lossless and dependency-preserving, at the cost of possibly retaining a little redundancy. Practical guidance: aim for BCNF; if the only BCNF option sacrifices a business-critical FD that you'd then have to enforce with expensive triggers, staying at 3NF for that table is a legitimate engineering choice.
How does dimensional modelling (star schema) deliberately violate normalization, and why is that correct for analytics?
A star schema has a central fact table (measurements, foreign keys to dimensions) surrounded by dimension tables that are intentionally denormalized — a date dimension stores year, quarter, month, day-name, is-holiday all in one wide row (transitive dependencies galore), and a product dimension embeds category and brand names rather than IDs. This is correct for OLAP because: queries are read-mostly (few or no updates, so update anomalies don't bite), analysts filter/group on dimension attributes directly (fewer joins → faster, simpler SQL), the query optimiser handles the star-join pattern specially, and dimensions are small relative to facts so the redundancy is cheap. Slowly-changing-dimension techniques (type 2 rows with validity ranges) handle the history that normalization would otherwise give you.

SQL Query Fundamentals

The logical evaluation order — get that right and the rest of SQL clicks.

Notes

Logical processing order

FROM / JOIN     -> produce the working row set
WHERE          -> filter individual rows (no aggregates yet)
GROUP BY       -> collapse into groups
HAVING         -> filter groups (can use aggregates)
SELECT         -> compute output columns, aliases, window functions
DISTINCT
ORDER BY       -> sort (can use SELECT aliases)
LIMIT / OFFSET -> slice

This is why you can't reference a SELECT alias in WHERE (WHERE runs first) but can in ORDER BY, and why aggregate filters go in HAVING not WHERE.

Aggregates & GROUP BY

  • COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)).
  • Every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY (standard SQL; some engines relax this).
  • HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to keep only groups meeting a condition.

Subqueries & CTEs

  • Scalar subquery (returns one value), IN (SELECT …), EXISTS (SELECT 1 …) (correlated, stops at first match — often faster than IN).
  • CTE (WITH x AS (…)) names a subquery for readability; recursive CTE walks hierarchies/graphs (org charts, bill of materials).

Window functions

SELECT name, dept, salary,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
       AVG(salary)  OVER (PARTITION BY dept)                      AS dept_avg,
       SUM(salary)  OVER (ORDER BY hire_date
                          ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)               AS running_total
FROM employees;

Windows compute per row without collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY). ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD, running sums, moving averages, "top N per group".

Cheat Sheet
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
  • WHERE filters rows (pre-aggregation); HAVING filters groups (post-aggregation).
  • SELECT aliases usable in ORDER BY, not in WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING (mostly).
  • Aggregates skip NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows regardless.
  • Every non-aggregated selected column must appear in GROUP BY.
  • EXISTS (correlated, short-circuits) often beats IN (subquery); beware NOT IN with NULLs (returns no rows).
  • CTE = named subquery; recursive CTE for hierarchies/graphs.
  • Window function = per-row calculation over a partition/frame; doesn't collapse rows.
  • Pagination: keyset (WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT n) scales better than OFFSET.
Q&A
Why can't you use a column alias defined in SELECT inside WHERE?
WHERE is evaluated before SELECT in the logical processing order, so the alias doesn't exist yet. Repeat the expression, or wrap the query in a subquery/CTE.
WHERE vs HAVING?
WHERE filters rows before grouping and can't reference aggregates. HAVING filters after grouping and is where aggregate conditions (SUM(x) > 100) go.
IN (subquery) vs EXISTS?
Both test membership. EXISTS is correlated and stops at the first matching row, often faster and NULL-safe. NOT IN with a subquery that can yield NULL is a trap — it returns no rows because the comparison becomes unknown; use NOT EXISTS.
What does a window function do that GROUP BY doesn't?
It computes an aggregate/ranking alongside each row without collapsing the result set, so you can show a salary and its department average on the same line.
Why prefer keyset pagination over OFFSET?
OFFSET n still scans and discards the first n rows, so page 10,000 is slow. Keyset ("seek") uses WHERE (sort_key) > (last_seen) with an index, so each page costs the same.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
HAVING.
Does AVG(col) include NULLs?
No — NULLs are skipped, so the average is over the non-NULL values only.
What runs first logically: FROM or WHERE?
FROM (and its joins) — it builds the row set that WHERE then filters.

Intermediate core

Second-highest salary in a table (handle ties and "no such row").
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp); — returns NULL if there's no second value. Or SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1. Or a window: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = 2.
Top 3 earners per department.
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r
  FROM employees
) t WHERE r <= 3;
DENSE_RANK keeps all ties at rank 3; use ROW_NUMBER for exactly 3 rows.

Advanced deep

Write a recursive CTE to list every subordinate of a manager in an employees(id, manager_id) table.
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees WHERE id = :manager
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT * FROM reports;
The anchor selects the root; the recursive term joins children of the current level; UNION ALL accumulates. Add a depth < N guard or cycle detection (UNION instead of UNION ALL, or track a path array) if the hierarchy might contain loops.
Explain the difference between ROWS and RANGE in a window frame, with a gotcha.
ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts physical rows — exactly the current row and the two before it. RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts rows whose ORDER BY value is within 2 of the current row's value — peer rows with the same sort value are all included together. Gotcha: the default frame when you specify ORDER BY but no frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which means a running SUM ... OVER (ORDER BY d) over data with duplicate d values includes all rows sharing the current d, not a per-row cumulative — often surprising. Specify ROWS explicitly for a true row-by-row running total.

Joins in Depth

The join types, the NULL edge cases, and the three algorithms underneath.

Notes

Join types

JoinReturns
INNER JOINOnly rows with a match on both sides.
LEFT [OUTER] JOINAll left rows; right columns NULL where no match.
RIGHT JOINMirror of LEFT (rarely used — just swap tables).
FULL OUTER JOINAll rows from both; NULLs where either side is missing.
CROSS JOINCartesian product (every left row × every right row).
Self joinA table joined to itself (employee–manager, adjacency).
Semi join (EXISTS)Left rows that have ≥ 1 match — no right columns, no duplication.
Anti join (NOT EXISTS)Left rows with no match.

NULL & predicate placement

  • A condition in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN filters the right table before joining (keeps unmatched left rows). The same condition in WHERE runs after the join and discards the NULL-extended left rows — effectively turning it into an inner join.
  • col = NULL never matches; joins compare with =, so NULL keys don't join.

Join algorithms (what the planner picks)

AlgorithmHowGood when
Nested loopfor each outer row, probe the inner (ideally via index)small outer side, indexed inner
Hash joinbuild a hash table on the smaller side, probe with the largerlarge unsorted inputs, equijoin, enough memory
Merge joinsort both by the join key, walk in lockstepinputs already sorted / indexed on the key, or range joins
Cheat Sheet
  • INNER = matches only. LEFT = all left + NULLs. FULL = all + NULLs both ways. CROSS = product.
  • RIGHT JOIN is just a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped — prefer LEFT for readability.
  • Filter on the joined (right) table: in ON to keep unmatched left rows, in WHERE to drop them.
  • WHERE right.col IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN = anti-join ("rows with no match").
  • Semi-join = EXISTS (no duplication); anti-join = NOT EXISTS.
  • NULL join keys never match (= NULL is unknown).
  • Planner chooses nested-loop (small + indexed), hash (big equijoin), or merge (sorted inputs).
  • Join order and predicates matter: index the join columns; filter early.
Q&A
INNER vs LEFT JOIN?
INNER returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT returns every row from the left table, filling right-side columns with NULL when there's no match.
Why does moving a condition from ON to WHERE change a LEFT JOIN's result?
In ON, the condition limits which right rows can match, but unmatched left rows still appear (with NULLs). In WHERE, it's applied after the join, and right.col = 'x' is false for the NULL-extended rows, so they're dropped — the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN.
How do you find rows in A with no corresponding row in B?
Anti-join: SELECT ... FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.k = B.k WHERE B.k IS NULL, or WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.k = A.k).
When does the optimizer choose a hash join?
For an equijoin on large, unsorted inputs when there's enough memory to build a hash table on the smaller side. It's O(n + m) versus nested loop's O(n × m) without an index.
What's a self join used for?
Relating rows within one table — employees to their managers, comparing consecutive rows, finding pairs (e.g. products with the same price), traversing an adjacency list one hop.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which join returns the Cartesian product?
CROSS JOIN (or an inner join with no join condition).
After a LEFT JOIN, how do you keep only the non-matching left rows?
WHERE right_table.key IS NULL.
Does a NULL in a join key match another NULL?
No. NULL = NULL is unknown, so those rows don't join.

Intermediate core

List all customers and their order count, including customers with zero orders.
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name;. COUNT(o.id) (not COUNT(*)) so no-order customers show 0, not 1.
A three-table join is slow. What do you check first?
EXPLAIN the plan: are the join columns indexed? Is there a full scan on a big table that a filter could use an index for? Is the estimated row count wildly off (stale statistics)? Is the join order sensible (small/filtered tables first)? Is a hash join spilling to disk (raise work_mem)? Are you accidentally producing a partial cross join (missing/incorrect ON condition)?

Advanced deep

Why is NOT IN (SELECT col FROM t) dangerous when col can be NULL, and what's the mechanism?
x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) is evaluated as x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL. The last term is unknown, so the whole conjunction can never be TRUE — it's either FALSE (if x matches something) or UNKNOWN. Result: the query returns zero rows the moment the subquery contains a single NULL, silently. Fixes: NOT EXISTS (uses = semantics per row and is NULL-safe here), add WHERE col IS NOT NULL to the subquery, or an anti-join with an explicit IS NULL check. This is one of the most common "the query worked in dev and returned nothing in prod" bugs.
Explain when a merge join beats a hash join even though both are O(n + m)-ish.
A hash join needs to build the whole hash table on one input (blocking, memory-hungry; spills to disk and degrades if it doesn't fit) and only supports equi-joins. A merge join needs both inputs sorted on the join key — but if they're already sorted (covering index on the key, or output of an earlier sort/merge), it does a single streaming pass with O(1) extra memory, produces output in sorted order (free for a downstream ORDER BY or another merge join), and handles range / inequality joins and band joins that hashing can't. So merge join wins for pre-sorted large inputs, pipelines of joins on the same key, and non-equijoins; hash join wins for ad hoc equijoins on unsorted data with enough RAM.

Indexes

The single biggest lever on query speed — and a tax on every write.

Notes

What an index is

A separate, ordered data structure mapping key values to row locations, so the engine can seek instead of scan. Turns O(n) lookups into O(log n). Costs storage and slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (every index must be maintained).

Index types

TypeGood for
B-treeDefault. Equality and range (<, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, prefix LIKE 'abc%').
HashEquality only, slightly faster for that; no ranges, no ordering.
BitmapLow-cardinality columns in analytics (Oracle); cheap AND/OR of predicates.
GiST / GIN / invertedFull-text, arrays, JSON, geospatial.

Clustered vs secondary

  • Clustered (InnoDB primary key, SQL Server): the table rows are stored in index order. One per table. Secondary indexes then store the PK value and do a second lookup.
  • Secondary / non-clustered: separate structure pointing back to the row (via PK or row id).
  • Covering index: contains every column the query needs (INCLUDE columns), so the engine never touches the table — "index-only scan".

Composite index column order

INDEX(a, b, c) serves WHERE a = ?, a = ? AND b = ?, a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ?, and a = ? AND b > ? — a left-most prefix. It does not help WHERE b = ? alone. Put equality columns first, then the range/sort column.

When NOT to index

Small tables, columns with very low cardinality (a boolean — unless combined), write-heavy tables where the index maintenance cost outweighs read benefit, columns wrapped in functions in the query (WHERE UPPER(name) = ? won't use a plain index — needs a functional/expression index), or leading-wildcard LIKE '%x'.

Cheat Sheet
  • Index = ordered lookup structure → seek not scan; O(log n) reads, slower writes + storage.
  • B-tree: equality + range + ordering + prefix LIKE 'x%'. Hash: equality only.
  • Clustered index = table stored in key order (one per table). Secondary indexes point back via PK.
  • Covering / index-only: index has all needed columns → no table access.
  • Composite index: usable only by a left-most prefix; equality columns first, range/sort last.
  • Function on the column (UPPER(x), x + 0) or leading % in LIKE → index not used (non-SARGable). Use an expression index or rewrite.
  • Don't index tiny tables, ultra-low-cardinality columns alone, or hot write paths without cause.
  • Check usage with EXPLAIN; drop unused indexes — they only cost.
Q&A
Why does an index speed up reads but slow down writes?
Reads use the ordered structure to jump straight to matching rows. Writes must additionally insert/move/delete entries in every index on the table, and can cause page splits — more I/O per modification.
What's a covering index?
An index that includes all columns a query references (in the key or as INCLUDE columns), so the query is answered entirely from the index without reading the table rows — an "index-only scan".
Given INDEX(country, city, name), which queries use it?
Anything filtering on a leftmost prefix: country=?; country=? AND city=?; country=? AND city=? AND name=?; country=? AND city>?. Not city=? alone, and not country=? AND name=? efficiently (it can seek on country then filter name).
Why doesn't WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 use an index on created_at?
The column is wrapped in a function, so the index's ordering of raw created_at values no longer maps to the predicate. Rewrite as a range: created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01', or create a functional index on YEAR(created_at).
Clustered vs non-clustered index?
Clustered defines the physical row order of the table (one allowed); a lookup lands directly on the row. Non-clustered is a separate structure whose leaf entries point to the row (via the clustering key or a row locator), often needing a second read.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Default index type in most relational databases?
B-tree.
How many clustered indexes can a table have?
One — it dictates the physical storage order of the rows.
Can a hash index support ORDER BY or range scans?
No — hash indexes only support equality lookups.

Intermediate core

A query filters on status = 'active' (5% of rows) and sorts by created_at. Best index?
INDEX(status, created_at). The equality on status narrows to the 5%, and because created_at is the next key column, the rows come out already sorted — no separate sort step. Add the selected columns as INCLUDE to make it covering.
You added five indexes and writes got much slower. How do you decide which to keep?
Look at index usage stats (pg_stat_user_indexes, sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats): drop indexes with zero or near-zero scans. Consolidate overlapping ones (an index on (a) is redundant if you have (a, b)). Keep only those that back real, frequent query patterns or FK/unique constraints. Measure write throughput before/after.

Advanced deep

Explain why random UUID primary keys hurt insert performance on a clustered index, and the mitigations.
With a clustered index, rows are stored in PK order. A monotonically increasing key (bigint identity) always inserts at the "right edge" — one hot page, sequential I/O, high fill. A random UUID inserts at random positions throughout the B-tree, causing constant page splits (a full page is torn in two to make room), index fragmentation, low page fill factor, more buffer-pool churn (every insert dirties a different page), and worse read locality later. Mitigations: use a time-ordered UUID (v7 / ULID / NEWSEQUENTIALID) so inserts are mostly append; keep the surrogate bigint as the clustered PK and store the UUID in a secondary unique index; or lower the fill factor to absorb splits (trades space for fewer splits).
What is a partial (filtered) index and when is it a big win?
An index with a WHERE predicate, so it only contains rows matching that condition (CREATE INDEX ... ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'). Wins when queries always target a small, well-defined subset: the index is far smaller (fits in cache, faster to scan/maintain), and writes to rows outside the predicate don't touch it at all. Classic uses: "active"/"pending"/"not deleted" flags where 99% of rows are the boring value, enforcing uniqueness only among non-deleted rows (UNIQUE ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and hot queues within a huge history table.

Query Planning & Optimization

How SQL (declarative) becomes an execution plan — and how to read it.

Notes

From SQL to plan

Parse → bind (resolve names/types) → logical plan (relational-algebra tree) → rewrite/normalize → cost-based optimization (enumerate plans, estimate cost) → physical plan (specific scan & join operators). SQL says what; the planner decides how.

Reading EXPLAIN

  • EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and shows real rows/time.
  • Look for: Seq Scan / Full Table Scan on a big table (often a missing index), estimated vs actual rows far apart (stale statistics → bad plan), expensive Sort or Hash spilling to disk, nested loop over many outer rows.
  • Cost is in arbitrary units; compare alternatives, don't read absolute values.

Cardinality estimation

The optimizer relies on statistics (row counts, column histograms, distinct-value estimates, correlation) to guess how many rows each operator produces. Bad estimates → wrong join algorithm/order. Keep stats fresh (ANALYZE / auto-stats); multi-column correlation often needs extended statistics.

Scan vs seek & SARGability

  • Index seek: navigate the B-tree to the matching range. Index/table scan: read everything.
  • A predicate is SARGable (Search-ARGument-able) if it can drive an index seek: col = ?, col > ?, col LIKE 'x%'. Non-SARGable: func(col) = ?, col + 1 = ?, col LIKE '%x', implicit type casts, OR across different columns.

Common fixes

Add/adjust an index; rewrite non-SARGable predicates; update statistics; break a giant query into steps / temp tables; add LIMIT; avoid SELECT * (prevents covering indexes); watch for implicit conversions (varchar column vs N'...' parameter).

Cheat Sheet
  • Pipeline: parse → bind → logical plan → cost-based optimize → physical plan.
  • EXPLAIN = estimate; EXPLAIN ANALYZE = run + measure. Compare estimated vs actual rows.
  • Red flags: seq/full scan on big tables, estimate wildly off actual, sort/hash spilling to disk, nested loop with a huge outer.
  • Optimizer decisions rely on statistics — keep them fresh; use extended/multi-column stats for correlated predicates.
  • SARGable predicate → index seek. func(col), col+1, leading %, implicit casts → scan.
  • Avoid SELECT * (blocks covering indexes, moves extra data).
  • Fixes: index it, rewrite the predicate, ANALYZE, simplify, add LIMIT, fix type mismatches.
Q&A
What's the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
EXPLAIN prints the planner's chosen plan with estimated costs and row counts without executing. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and shows actual timing and row counts alongside the estimates — the gap between them reveals bad statistics.
Why does the optimizer need statistics?
To estimate how many rows each filter/join produces, which determines the best join algorithm and order. Without accurate stats it might pick a nested loop expecting 10 rows when there are 10 million.
What makes a predicate non-SARGable?
Anything that stops the engine from using the index's key ordering: a function or arithmetic on the column, a leading wildcard in LIKE, an implicit type conversion on the column side, or ORing conditions on different columns.
Your query's plan changed overnight and got slow. Likely cause?
Statistics changed (auto-stats update after a big data load), data distribution shifted, or parameter-sniffing produced a plan optimal for one parameter value but bad for another. Also: an index was dropped, or the DB was upgraded.
Why avoid SELECT * for performance?
It forces the engine to fetch every column from the base table, defeating covering indexes (index-only scans), increasing I/O and network transfer, and breaking if the schema changes.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a "Seq Scan" / "Full Table Scan" in a plan usually indicate?
The engine is reading every row because no useful index exists for the query's predicate (or the optimizer thinks a scan is cheaper, e.g. the filter matches most rows).
Is SQL imperative or declarative?
Declarative — you state the result you want; the query planner decides the execution strategy.
Command to refresh a table's statistics (PostgreSQL)?
ANALYZE table_name; (or VACUUM ANALYZE).

Intermediate core

Rewrite WHERE substring(phone, 1, 3) = '415' to be SARGable.
WHERE phone >= '415' AND phone < '416' (range on the raw column), assuming phone is stored as text with the area code first. Or add a functional index on substring(phone, 1, 3). The point is to let the index on phone drive a seek.
Plan shows "estimated rows: 1, actual rows: 2,000,000" on a join input. What now?
The optimizer badly under-estimated, likely picking a nested loop that's now catastrophic. Update statistics; if the mis-estimate is from correlated columns (city + state), add multi-column/extended statistics. If it's a complex expression, materialise it or add a stats object on it. As a stopgap, a query hint to force a hash join or a different order.

Advanced deep

Explain parameter sniffing and the strategies to deal with it.
On first execution of a parameterised query/prepared statement, the optimizer "sniffs" the actual parameter values and builds a plan optimal for them, then caches and reuses that plan. If later executions pass values with very different selectivity (e.g. first call filters country = 'VA' = 0.1% of rows → index seek plan; later call country = 'US' = 60% → that seek plan does millions of random lookups), performance tanks. Strategies: OPTIMIZE FOR a representative value or OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN (use average density); RECOMPILE the statement each run (trades CPU for a fresh plan); split into separate queries/branches per data shape; disable parameter sniffing at DB or query level; use plan guides / forced plans for the known-good one. Postgres mitigates this with its "custom vs generic plan" heuristic after 5 executions.
Why is join-order selection hard, and how do optimizers bound the search?
The number of possible join orders for n tables grows factorially (n! left-deep, more counting bushy trees), and each order's cost depends on cardinality estimates that compound error at each step. Optimizers bound it with: dynamic programming over subsets (System R style, exact but 2ⁿ — practical to ~12 tables), then heuristic search (greedy, genetic — Postgres's GEQO) beyond a threshold; restricting to left-deep trees to shrink the space; pruning dominated sub-plans; and pushing selections/projections down first so estimates are on smaller inputs. Even so, a 20-table query can get a poor order, which is why breaking huge queries up, providing hints, or using materialised intermediates is sometimes necessary.

Transactions & ACID

All-or-nothing units of work, and the four guarantees that make them safe.

Notes

ACID

PropertyMeans
AAtomicityAll statements commit or none do. A failure rolls back everything.
CConsistencyA transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another — constraints, FKs, triggers hold at commit.
IIsolationConcurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted (or, at higher levels, in-flight) changes.
DDurabilityOnce committed, the change survives crash / power loss (flushed to non-volatile storage).

How the engine delivers it

  • Atomicity + Durability — write-ahead logging (WAL / redo log): log the change durably before modifying data pages. On crash, redo committed transactions, undo uncommitted ones.
  • Isolation — locking (2PL) or multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) — see the Locking topic.
  • Consistency — constraint checking + the app writing correct logic; the DB enforces the declared rules.

Transaction control

BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
  SAVEPOINT s1;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
  -- ROLLBACK TO s1;   -- partial undo
COMMIT;               -- or ROLLBACK;

Auto-commit mode wraps each statement in its own transaction. Long-running transactions hold resources (locks, old row versions) — keep them short.

Distributed transactions

Across databases/services, atomicity needs two-phase commit (prepare → commit), which blocks if the coordinator fails. Many systems avoid it with the Saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions plus compensating actions to undo earlier steps on failure (eventual consistency, not atomic).

Cheat Sheet
  • Atomicity: all-or-nothing (rollback on failure). Consistency: valid state → valid state (constraints hold). Isolation: concurrent txns don't interfere. Durability: committed = survives a crash.
  • WAL / redo log: log durably before touching data pages → atomicity + durability + crash recovery (redo committed, undo in-flight).
  • BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK; SAVEPOINT + ROLLBACK TO for partial undo.
  • Keep transactions short — long ones hold locks and bloat old-version storage.
  • Cross-service atomicity: 2PC (blocking, coordinator SPOF) or Sagas (compensating actions, eventual consistency).
  • Consistency in ACID (constraints) ≠ consistency in CAP (replica agreement).
Q&A
What does atomicity guarantee?
A transaction's statements all take effect together or not at all. If any step fails (or you ROLLBACK), the database is left as if the transaction never ran.
How does a database provide durability without an fsync on every data page?
Write-ahead logging: it appends the change to a sequential log and fsyncs that before acknowledging commit. Data pages are flushed lazily later; if the server crashes, recovery replays the log to reconstruct committed changes.
Is "Consistency" in ACID the same as in CAP?
No. ACID consistency = the database's own integrity rules (constraints, triggers, FKs) hold after each transaction. CAP consistency = all replicas return the same latest value (linearizability). Different concerns.
What is a savepoint for?
A named point within a transaction you can partially roll back to (ROLLBACK TO savepoint) without aborting the whole transaction — useful for retrying a sub-step or handling an expected error.
Why is two-phase commit avoided in microservices?
It's a blocking protocol: if the coordinator crashes after "prepare", participants hold locks indefinitely; it couples service availability and hurts throughput. Sagas trade atomicity for availability, using compensating transactions to undo prior steps.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Expand ACID.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
What log ensures a committed transaction survives a crash?
The write-ahead log (WAL) / redo log — written and flushed before commit is acknowledged.
What statement discards all changes in the current transaction?
ROLLBACK.

Intermediate core

Walk through crash recovery using the WAL.
On restart, the engine reads the log from the last checkpoint. Redo phase: re-apply every logged change (committed or not) to bring pages up to the log's end. Undo phase: for transactions that were active (no COMMIT record) at crash time, walk their log records backward and apply the compensating (undo) records, writing CLRs so undo is itself idempotent. Result: committed work is present, uncommitted work is gone. (This is ARIES.)
A money transfer debits account A and credits B. Which ACID properties are at stake if the server crashes mid-way?
Atomicity (must not leave A debited without B credited — roll back on recovery) and Durability (once the transfer commits, both effects must persist through the crash). Isolation matters for concurrent transfers reading the balances; Consistency for a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint.

Advanced deep

What durability guarantees do you actually get, and where can they silently weaken?
"Durable" means the commit record survived to stable storage — but the chain has weak links: the DB may be configured for group commit / delayed fsync (synchronous_commit=off, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2) trading a few ms of committed data for throughput; the OS page cache may buffer the write; the disk's own write cache may lie about fsync unless barriers/FUA are honoured; on a single node a disk failure still loses everything. Real durability for important data means synchronous replication to another node/AZ (so a quorum has the commit) plus verified fsync behaviour and battery-backed/enterprise storage. Interview point: "durable" is a spectrum set by configuration and topology, not a binary the DB gives you for free.
Compare the Saga pattern's orchestration vs choreography styles.
Orchestration: a central saga coordinator explicitly invokes each service's local transaction and, on failure, invokes the compensations in reverse. Pros: the workflow is in one place, easy to reason about, add steps, and monitor; clear timeout/retry handling. Cons: the orchestrator is a component to build and scale, and can become a hidden monolith of business logic. Choreography: each service reacts to events and emits its own; there's no central controller. Pros: loose coupling, no single bottleneck, services evolve independently. Cons: the end-to-end flow is implicit and spread across services (hard to see, debug, or change), risk of cyclic event dependencies, and compensation ordering is harder to guarantee. Rule of thumb: choreography for 2–4 simple steps; orchestration once the workflow has branching, many steps, or needs observability.

Isolation Levels & Anomalies

The dial between "fast but weird" and "correct but contended".

Notes

The read anomalies

AnomalyWhat happens
Dirty readYou read another transaction's uncommitted change (which may roll back).
Non-repeatable readYou read a row twice in one transaction and get different values (someone committed an update between).
Phantom readYou run the same range query twice and new rows appear/disappear (someone inserted/deleted matching rows).
Lost updateTwo transactions read-modify-write the same row; one overwrites the other's change.
Write skewTwo transactions read an overlapping set, each makes a decision valid alone, but together they violate an invariant.

The SQL standard levels

LevelPrevents
Read Uncommitted(nothing — dirty reads allowed)
Read Committeddirty reads
Repeatable Read+ non-repeatable reads
Serializable+ phantoms; result equivalent to some serial order

Reality check: the standard defines levels by which anomalies they forbid, but engines implement them differently. PostgreSQL "Read Committed" is the default; its "Repeatable Read" is actually snapshot isolation (also blocks phantoms but allows write skew); its "Serializable" adds SSI (serializable snapshot isolation) to catch write skew. Oracle's max is snapshot isolation labelled "Serializable". Know your engine.

Choosing

Higher isolation → more locking / more aborts / lower throughput. Most OLTP runs at Read Committed and handles lost updates explicitly (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic version columns, atomic UPDATE ... SET x = x + 1). Use Serializable for logic where correctness under concurrency is subtle and you'd rather retry than reason.

Cheat Sheet
  • Dirty read: see uncommitted data. Non-repeatable read: same row changes mid-transaction. Phantom: same range query returns different row sets.
  • Read Uncommitted → allows all. Read Committed → no dirty reads. Repeatable Read → + no non-repeatable reads. Serializable → + no phantoms, as-if-serial.
  • Lost update & write skew are not in the classic table but matter — snapshot isolation still allows write skew.
  • Postgres default = Read Committed; its "Repeatable Read" = snapshot isolation; "Serializable" = SSI.
  • Higher level = more aborts/blocking, less throughput.
  • Prevent lost updates at Read Committed with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic version column, or atomic in-place update.
Q&A
Dirty read vs non-repeatable read?
Dirty read: you see data another transaction hasn't committed (and might roll back). Non-repeatable read: you see data that was committed, but it changed between your two reads within the same transaction.
What is a phantom read?
Re-running a range/predicate query in the same transaction returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching your predicate.
Which anomaly does Repeatable Read not prevent (in the standard)?
Phantom reads. (Many MVCC implementations of Repeatable Read do prevent phantoms via snapshots but then allow write skew.)
What is write skew and which level stops it?
Two transactions read an overlapping data set, each individually preserves an invariant, but their combined writes break it (e.g. both doctors go off-call because each sees the other still on-call). Only true Serializable (e.g. Postgres SSI or strict 2PL) prevents it; snapshot isolation does not.
How do you prevent a lost update at Read Committed?
Lock the row on read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use an atomic update (UPDATE t SET n = n + 1 WHERE id = ?), or optimistic concurrency: read a version/timestamp, then UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? and retry if zero rows changed.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
Read Uncommitted.
What's the strongest standard isolation level?
Serializable — the outcome is equivalent to running the transactions one at a time in some order.
Default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
Read Committed.

Intermediate core

Two users book the last seat at the same time; both succeed. Which anomaly, and how do you fix it?
A lost update (or write skew, depending on the check). Fixes: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat row so the second transaction blocks; a unique constraint on (event, seat) so the second insert fails; an atomic conditional update UPDATE seats SET taken = true WHERE id = ? AND taken = false and check the row count; or Serializable isolation with retry.
Why might raising isolation to Serializable make throughput worse without any errors?
More lock contention (strict 2PL) — transactions wait longer for shared/exclusive locks and range locks — or, under SSI, more transactions get aborted with serialization failures and must retry, wasting the work already done. Both reduce effective throughput even though every committed result is correct.

Advanced deep

Explain how PostgreSQL's Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) catches write skew that plain snapshot isolation misses.
SSI runs transactions on snapshots (like Repeatable Read) but additionally tracks read/write dependencies between concurrent transactions using predicate locks (SIReadLocks) on the rows and index ranges each transaction reads. A non-serializable execution always contains a specific pattern: a "dangerous structure" of two consecutive rw-antidependency edges (T1 reads something T2 writes, and T2 reads something T3 writes) forming a cycle in the dependency graph. When the engine detects a transaction that is the "pivot" of such a structure, it aborts one of them with a serialization failure at commit time. So write skew — which is exactly a cycle of rw-dependencies with no ww-conflict — is caught, at the cost of tracking reads and occasional false-positive aborts. Applications must be prepared to retry on 40001.
What is the "read committed" behaviour on a row that gets updated by another transaction mid-statement, and how does it differ between engines?
Under Read Committed, each statement sees a fresh snapshot. If an UPDATE ... WHERE in transaction B tries to modify a row that concurrent transaction A has updated but not committed, B blocks until A ends. If A commits, PostgreSQL then re-evaluates B's WHERE against A's new version ("EvalPlanQual" / update-chasing) — if it still matches, B updates the new version; if not, B skips it. This can produce non-serializable results and even "lost update"-like surprises where B's WHERE saw the old value but wrote based on it. Oracle behaves similarly with statement-level restart. MySQL (InnoDB) Read Committed releases locks after each statement and also re-reads. The subtle, engine-specific point: at Read Committed, a single multi-row UPDATE is not a consistent point-in-time operation under concurrency — use FOR UPDATE or a higher level when that matters.

Locking, MVCC & Deadlocks

Two strategies for isolation — block writers, or keep multiple versions.

Notes

Lock-based concurrency

  • Shared (S) lock for reads, Exclusive (X) for writes. S–S compatible; anything with X conflicts.
  • Two-Phase Locking (2PL): a growing phase (acquire locks) then a shrinking phase (release, no new acquires). Guarantees serializability. Strict 2PL holds all locks until commit/abort — also prevents cascading aborts.
  • Granularity: row → page → table. Fine locks = more concurrency but more overhead; the engine may escalate to a coarser lock under memory pressure.
  • Intent locks (IS/IX) on the table signal "I hold row locks below", so a table-level lock request can detect the conflict without scanning every row.

MVCC

Each write creates a new version of the row tagged with the transaction's id/timestamp; readers see the version consistent with their snapshot. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Used by PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL/InnoDB, SQL Server (RCSI). Cost: old versions accumulate and must be cleaned up (VACUUM in Postgres, undo/purge in InnoDB); long transactions hold back cleanup and bloat storage.

Deadlocks

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs — a cycle in the wait-for graph. The engine detects the cycle and aborts a victim (usually the one with least work done), which the app must retry.

  • Prevent by acquiring locks in a consistent order everywhere, keeping transactions short, using lower isolation where safe, and adding indexes so updates lock fewer rows.

Explicit locking

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (X lock the read rows), FOR SHARE, SKIP LOCKED (job queues — grab the next unlocked row), NOWAIT (fail instead of wait), advisory locks.

Cheat Sheet
  • S lock (read) compatible with S; X lock (write) conflicts with everything.
  • 2PL → serializable; strict 2PL holds locks to commit (no cascading aborts).
  • Lock granularity row/page/table; engine may escalate under pressure; intent locks (IX/IS) coordinate levels.
  • MVCC: writes make new versions; readers use a snapshot → readers don't block writers or vice versa.
  • MVCC cost: dead-tuple/undo cleanup (VACUUM/purge); long transactions block it → bloat.
  • Deadlock = cycle in wait-for graph → engine kills a victim → app retries.
  • Avoid deadlocks: consistent lock ordering, short transactions, proper indexes, lower isolation if safe.
  • FOR UPDATE / SKIP LOCKED / NOWAIT for explicit control (e.g. queue workers).
Q&A
What's the core advantage of MVCC over pure locking?
Reads don't take locks and don't block writes (and aren't blocked by them) — each reader sees a consistent snapshot from its start time. This dramatically improves read-heavy concurrency.
What does the second "phase" in two-phase locking refer to?
The shrinking phase: once a transaction releases any lock it may not acquire another. (Strict 2PL just defers all releases to commit/abort.) It's unrelated to two-phase commit.
What causes a deadlock and how does the DB resolve it?
A cycle where each transaction waits on a lock held by another. The engine's deadlock detector finds the cycle and aborts one transaction (the victim) with a deadlock error; the application retries it.
Why can long-running transactions hurt an MVCC database even if they're read-only?
The old row versions visible to that transaction's snapshot can't be garbage-collected while it runs, so dead tuples / undo logs accumulate, tables and indexes bloat, and vacuum/purge falls behind — degrading everyone's performance.
What is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED good for?
Concurrent job queues: each worker grabs the next available (unlocked) row, skipping rows other workers have locked, so N workers pull distinct jobs without blocking each other.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Are two shared locks on the same row compatible?
Yes — multiple readers can hold S locks simultaneously. An X lock conflicts with any other lock.
In MVCC, does a writer block a reader?
No. The reader sees an older committed version from its snapshot while the writer creates a new one.
What does the database do when it detects a deadlock?
Aborts one transaction (the victim) and returns a deadlock error; that transaction must be retried.

Intermediate core

Your service gets frequent deadlocks on two tables A and B. First thing to change?
Make every code path lock A before B (a consistent global ordering), so no cycle can form. Also shorten the transactions, ensure the UPDATEs use indexed predicates (so they lock few rows), and consider batching in a fixed key order.
What is lock escalation and when does it bite?
When a transaction holds many row/page locks, the engine may convert them to a single table lock to save memory. It bites during large bulk UPDATE/DELETE: suddenly the whole table is locked and concurrent access stalls. Mitigate by batching the operation into smaller chunks, or (SQL Server) disabling escalation for that table.

Advanced deep

How do gap locks / next-key locks in InnoDB Repeatable Read prevent phantoms, and what's the downside?
